tool.name: BlurredHillshade
tool.summary: Computes a deliberately softened (blurred) hillshade from a single-band DEM - the blurring component of the classic Swiss method. Blur the DEM before shading (default) or the finished hillshade after, with a radius in cells or ground units (sized geodesically per row on geographic rasters). Includes all the Enhanced Hillshade options.
tool.usage:
Some people like to blur a hillshade so that it is visually softer and aesthetically less distracting. Kurt Brassel, who first automated the Swiss cartographers' hand-drawn relief conventions, argued that small terrain features carry too little information for their shading to be trustworthy - their shading tends to be "fictive" or "creative" - and so should be de-emphasized by blurring; the USGS uses a blurred hillshade on its topo maps. Not everybody agrees that blurred hillshades are more attractive, though, so give the result some careful thought before you apply it.
The tool offers two ways to blur, selected by the What to blur parameter. Blurring the DEM first (the default) averages the elevations within the radius and computes the hillshade from that smoothed terrain: small landforms are removed from the terrain itself, larger forms keep crisp shading, and cast shadows and hypsometric shading follow the generalized surface - this usually looks a little better. Blurring the hillshade afterward computes the normal hillshade and then blurs the finished image: every tonal edge softens, including cast-shadow boundaries (a soft penumbra effect), closer to a photographic blur.
The blur radius can be given in cells or in ground units (meters, kilometers, feet, or miles). Ground-unit radii are converted to cells planarly for projected rasters, and per row on the spheroid (geodesic) for geographic (latitude/longitude) rasters, so the neighborhood stays true at any latitude. The blur is a NoData-ignoring circular mean: NoData cells stay NoData, and cells near data edges average whatever valid neighbors fall inside the radius. The appropriate radius depends on the raster resolution and your display scale - expect to try several values before settling on one you like. Blurring requires reading the whole DEM into memory at once.
Everything else works exactly like the Enhanced Hillshade: correct on geographic DEMs via per-row spheroidal cell dimensions, elevation units read from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when defined, gray levels, hypsometric shading, vertical exaggeration, and modeled cast shadows.
This tool is one part of the classic "Swiss style" of relief presentation (after Eduard Imhof and the Swiss cartographers, whose hand-drawn conventions Kurt Brassel first automated), which combines three strategies: illuminating the terrain from multiple directions, elevation-based tone adjustments that mimic atmospheric perspective, and softening of the final image. In this toolbox the MDOW Hillshade and Multi-Sun Hillshade tools provide the multi-directional illumination, the hypsometric-shading options and the Simple Hypsometric Shading tool provide the elevation-based tinting, and the Blurred Hillshade tool provides the softening.
By default the output matches the input grid exactly (same extent, cell size, and coordinate system). Honored environments: Processing Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Output Coordinate System, all applied as finishing steps to the computed hillshade - the extent clips it (with the snap raster aligning the clip window), the cell size resamples it, and the output coordinate system reprojects it. Because the shading is always computed first from the full-resolution source DEM, cells at a clipped edge carry true hillshade values, and resampling or reprojecting smooths the finished shading rather than recomputing it on the new grid. The Mask environment is not honored, and pyramids are always built with bilinear resampling regardless of the Pyramid environment. The output carries statistics and a histogram so it renders correctly without a separate Calculate Statistics step. Reference: Horn, B. K. P. 1981. Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE 69:14-47.
The output arrives drawn in a black-to-white stretch in which white is the highest value present, or, with 32 or fewer gray levels, in unique values with one gray for each level.

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute the blurred hillshade from. It must be single band. Choose a raster from the map or browse to one on disk.
The output blurred hillshade raster (integer, 0 to one less than the number of gray levels; NoData where the DEM has NoData or at the outer edge). A suggested name is filled in from the input.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Set automatically, and hidden in the dialog, when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system or is in geographic coordinates (geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters). You are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say.

How far the blur reaches around each cell, in the blur radius units. Larger radii give a blurrier, more generalized result. The appropriate value depends on the raster resolution and how zoomed in your map or layout is - you will almost certainly try several values before you settle on one you like. The default is 10. A radius smaller than one cell blurs nothing; the tool warns when that happens.

The units of the blur radius. Cells applies the same radius everywhere. Meters, Kilometers, Feet, and Miles are converted to cells from the raster's cell size - planarly for projected rasters, and per row on the spheroid (geodesic) for geographic rasters, so the neighborhood stays true at any latitude.

Which surface the blur is applied to. DEM (blur before shading), the default, averages the elevations first and computes the hillshade from the smoothed terrain: small landforms are removed from the terrain itself while larger forms keep crisp shading, and cast shadows and hypsometric shading follow the generalized surface - this usually looks a little better. Hillshade (blur after shading) computes the normal hillshade first and then blurs the finished image: every tonal edge softens, including cast-shadow boundaries (a soft penumbra effect), for a look closer to a photographic blur.

How cells within the radius are weighted in the mean. Average (the default) weights every cell in the circular neighborhood equally, matching the classic Focal Statistics recipe. Gaussian weights cells by distance from the center (sigma = half the radius, truncated at the radius), giving a smoother falloff that avoids the faint box-like artifacts a uniform average can leave at larger radii.
The compass direction of the light source, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north. The default 315 (northwest) is the cartographic convention.
The angle of the light source above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees. The default is 45.

The number of gray levels in the output: values run from 0 (fully shaded) to one less than this number (fully lit), each value covering an equal share of the illumination range. The default, 256, matches the standard Esri hillshade's 0 to 255. A small number gives a posterized cartographic look; with 32 or fewer levels the output also gets a raster attribute table listing each gray level and its cell count. A larger number gives a higher-precision hillshade, although the added precision may not be visually apparent on a computer screen.
Darkens the hillshade at lower elevations to add an impression of overall relief. The amount is set by the hypsometric strength.

How strongly low elevations are darkened, 0 to 100 percent. At strength s, the brightness multiplier grades from (100 - s) percent at the minimum elevation up to 100 percent at the maximum. The default is 50.
Multiplies the elevations before shading, exaggerating (greater than 1) or flattening (less than 1) the relief. The default is 1 (no exaggeration).

Dims terrain that is hidden from the sun behind other topography to a percentage of its unshadowed value, set by the shadow brightness parameter. With the DEM blurred before shading, shadows are cast by the generalized terrain; with the hillshade blurred after, shadow edges are softened by the blur.

The percentage of its unshadowed hillshade value that a shadowed cell keeps, 0 to 100. Use 0 for fully black shadows or larger values to keep relief detail visible inside the shadows. The default is 20.

scriptExample.title: Blurred Hillshade example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Blur the DEM with a 250-meter Gaussian kernel before shading.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.BlurredHillshade( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_Blurred", elev_units="Meters", blur_radius=250, radius_units="Meters", blur_target="DEM (blur before shading)", kernel="Gaussian", azimuth=315, altitude=45, levels=256)

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Deliberately softened (blurred) hillshade - the blurring component of the Swiss method - with the blur applied to the DEM before shading or to the finished hillshade after, and correct geodesic handling of geographic DEMs.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes a blurred (smoothed) hillshade from a single-band DEM: a circular NoData-ignoring mean of a user-chosen radius (cells, meters, kilometers, feet, or miles; ground-unit radii sized per row on the spheroid for geographic rasters) is applied either to the DEM before shading (default - generalizes the terrain itself, de-emphasizing small features whose shading the data cannot support) or to the finished hillshade image (softens every tonal edge including cast-shadow boundaries). Kernel weighting is a uniform average or a Gaussian. All Enhanced Hillshade options are included: gray levels, hypsometric shading, vertical exaggeration, and modeled cast shadows. The output matches the input grid (honoring the Processing Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Output Coordinate System environments as post-computation finishing steps) and carries statistics and a histogram.
dataIdInfo.idCredit: Tool by Jeff Jenness, Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Gradient method: Horn, B. K. P. 1981. Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE 69:14-47. Suggested citation: Jenness, J. (2026). Blurred Hillshade. Jenness Enterprises Wildlife and Forestry Tools for ArcGIS Pro. Available at: http://www.jennessent.com.
